# Intrinsic mixed half-depth forces central symmetry

Let C be compact and convex in R^n x R^d, let

    S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d), q=dim_H(S)>0,
    mu=H_q restricted to S, M=mu(S)>0.

The integer fibers need not have one common affine direction space.
For ANY actual point y=(j,c) in S, the following are equivalent:

  1. Every closed ambient halfspace containing y has mu mass at least M/2.
  2. The angular pushforward of mu about y is antipodally invariant.
  3. The full mixed measure mu is centrally symmetric about y.
  4. H_q(S intersect (2y-S))=M.

In this event the normalized depth is exactly one half and y is the
true full ambient centroid. The conclusion concerns the measure;
unmatched lower-dimensional fibers can prevent set symmetry.

The proof below gives a complete injectivity argument for the odd
hemisphere transform and treats the changing intrinsic affine spans.
No OC depth bound follows from this characterization.

## 1. Odd hemisphere-transform injectivity by Gaussian moments

Let N>=1 and let sigma be a finite signed Borel measure on the unit
sphere S^(N-1). Suppose

    T(u)=integral sign(u dot theta) dsigma(theta)=0

for almost every u on the sphere. Then sigma is antipodally invariant.
Equivalently, the hemisphere transform is injective on odd finite
measures. Values assigned to sign(0) do not affect this assertion;
take sign(0)=0.

Here is an elementary proof. Let G be a standard Gaussian vector in
R^N. Its direction is uniform and independent of its positive length,
so T(G)=0 almost surely. For a unit vector v and the probabilists'
Hermite polynomials H_m, defined by

    exp(tx-t^2/2)=sum_(m>=0) H_m(x)t^m/m!,

we therefore have

    0=E[T(G) H_m(v dot G)].                          (1)

For fixed unit theta put Z=theta dot G and rho=v dot theta. Conditional
Gaussian expectation of the generating function gives

    E[H_m(v dot G) | Z]=rho^m H_m(Z).

Indeed the conditional generating function is
`exp(t rho Z-t^2 rho^2/2)`; comparison of coefficients proves the
identity, including rho=+1 or -1. Fubini in (1) is valid since sigma
is finite and the absolute Gaussian polynomial moment is finite. Thus

    0=c_m integral (v dot theta)^m dsigma(theta),
    c_m=E[sign(Z)H_m(Z)].                            (2)

For odd m=2k+1, c_m is nonzero. Writing phi for the standard normal
density and using `(phi H_(m-1))'=-phi H_m` gives

    c_(2k+1)=2 integral_0^infinity H_(2k+1)(z)phi(z)dz
             =2phi(0)H_(2k)(0)
             =2phi(0)(-1)^k(2k-1)!! !=0,             (3)

with (-1)!!=1. Hence every odd directional polynomial moment of sigma
vanishes. Homogeneity extends this to arbitrary v, and expanding the
polynomial in v shows that every odd monomial moment vanishes.

Let sigma^a be the image of sigma under theta -> -theta. The measure
sigma-sigma^a has zero even polynomial moments by parity and zero odd
polynomial moments by (2)--(3). Polynomial restrictions are uniformly
dense among continuous functions on the compact sphere, by
Stone--Weierstrass. The finite signed measure sigma-sigma^a is therefore
zero. This proves the claim without requiring an angular density or
smoothness of the measure.

## 2. Half-depth and angular evenness

Since q>0, the point y has zero mu mass. Push mu forward by

    a -> (a-y)/|a-y|

to obtain a finite angular measure nu of mass M. For almost every
Gaussian normal G, the hyperplane through y with normal G is mu-null.
To see this, for every fixed a!=y the scalar G dot (a-y) is a nondegenerate
Gaussian and vanishes with probability zero; integrate by Fubini.

If y has depth at least M/2, the two opposite closed through-y caps for
such a normal both have mass at least M/2 and sum to M. Both therefore
have mass exactly M/2, so the sign transform of nu vanishes almost
everywhere. Section 1 makes nu antipodally invariant.

Conversely, an even angular measure puts at least M/2 in every closed
hemisphere, since opposite closed hemispheres cover the sphere and
have equal measure. Hence every closed through-y halfspace has mass at
least M/2. Every containing halfspace contains its parallel through-y
halfspace. A generic mu-null through-y boundary gives equality, so the
depth is exactly one half. This establishes equivalence of statements
1 and 2 for the present source; this step itself uses only mu({y})=0.

## 3. Primitive lattice rays and their injective angular charts

For a nonzero primitive integer vector v, consider the two base rays

    j+k v and j-k v, k=1,2,... .

Choose one orientation for each unoriented primitive line represented
by a nonempty integer fiber. Only finitely many directions matter.
Write K_z={x:(z,x) in C}, and define compact convex slope sets

    A_k=(K_(j+kv)-c)/k,
    B_k=(c-K_(j-kv))/k,                              (4)

with missing fibers interpreted as empty. Convexity and (j,c) in C give

    A_1 contains A_2 contains ...,
    B_1 contains B_2 contains ....                   (5)

For example if k<ell and x in K_(j+ell v), the convex combination
`c+(k/ell)(x-c)` belongs to K_(j+kv), proving the first nesting.

The chart

    Phi_v(s)=(v,s)/sqrt(|v|^2+|s|^2),  s in R^d,    (6)

is injective and is a homeomorphism onto the angular stratum whose
nonzero base coordinate is a positive multiple of v. Distinct primitive
oriented base rays have disjoint strata; the own-fiber angular stratum,
where the base coordinate is zero, is disjoint from all of them.

Scaling a q-dimensional fiber by 1/k changes its H_q measure by k^(-q).
Thus the angular source on the positive stratum is precisely

    (Phi_v)_# [sum_(k>=1) k^q H_q restricted to A_k].

The antipodal image of the negative-stratum source is the same expression
with B_k. No angular surface Jacobian is assumed: these are pushforward
MEASURES under the same injective chart. Evenness of nu therefore gives
the exact measure identity on R^d

    sum_(k>=1) k^q H_q|A_k
       =sum_(k>=1) k^q H_q|B_k.                     (7)

Every nonempty integer fiber has affine dimension at most q. Fibers of
smaller dimension contribute zero to (7), exactly as to mu.

## 4. Aligning intrinsic spaces and recovering every positive fiber

Suppose the left side of (7) has positive mass. By nesting, A_1 has
positive q-volume, and all positive-volume A_k share the q-dimensional
affine span of A_1: a contained q-dimensional convex set has the same
span. All later lower-dimensional A_k are also contained in that span.
The same holds on the right, whose total mass is positive by (7).

The two affine q-planes must agree. If they were different, their
intersection would have dimension at most q-1 (or be empty), and their
restricted H_q measures would be mutually singular, contrary to equality
of the positive measures in (7). Call their common affine plane L_aff.

Relative to its Euclidean H_q measure, (7) says

    sum_(k>=1) k^q 1_(A_k)(s)
       =sum_(k>=1) k^q 1_(B_k)(s)    almost everywhere. (8)

By (5), at any s each active index set is a prefix. Its density value
is consequently `S_q(r)=sum_(k=1)^r k^q`, where r is the prefix length.
These values strictly increase in r. Equation (8) forces equal prefix
lengths and hence `1_(A_k)=1_(B_k)` almost everywhere for every k.

In particular the positive-volume indices agree on both sides. For
each such index, A_k and B_k are compact convex sets of full relative
dimension q in L_aff. Such sets that agree almost everywhere agree
exactly: a point in one and outside the other, joined to a relative
interior ball of the first, would produce positive q-volume difference.
Thus every positive fiber on this primitive line satisfies

    K_(j-kv)=2c-K_(j+kv).                            (9)

If one side of (7) has zero mass, the other does too, so this direction
has no positive fiber to recover. Applying the argument to all primitive
lines recovers all positive fibers away from the own base j, while
retaining the full affine-space bookkeeping.

## 5. The own fiber by polar coordinates

If K_j has positive q-volume, let L=lin(K_j-K_j). Since c belongs to K_j,
the translated body K_j-c lies in L and is star-shaped about zero.
Let rho(theta) be its radial extent in direction theta in S(L), allowing
rho=0 when c is on the relative boundary. Polar integration in L shows
that its angular pushforward has density

    rho(theta)^q/q

with respect to surface measure on S(L). For q=1, S(L) consists of two
points with their counting surface measure, and the same formula holds.
Evenness on this own-fiber angular stratum implies
`rho(theta)^q=rho(-theta)^q` almost everywhere. Since q>0, the radial
extents agree almost everywhere, so K_j and 2c-K_j agree up to q-volume
zero. Their full-dimensional relative convexity and closedness imply
exact equality.

The own fiber is indeed positive. If all positive source mass were
already at j, this is immediate. Otherwise (9) provides a positive
reflected pair at j+kv,j-kv. Their Minkowski midpoint contains a relative
q-dimensional neighborhood of c in their common direction space, and
is contained in K_j by convexity. Hence K_j has positive q-volume.
This also shows why no unsupported assumption about the own section's
affine dimension has entered the proof.

Together with (9), own-fiber symmetry proves statement 3. Statements
3 and 4 are equivalent by reflection invariance and equality of total
finite mass, and a centrally symmetric finite measure has depth at
least one half at its center. This completes all four equivalences.

In particular c is in the relative interior of the own positive fiber.
All full first moments exist, and reflection invariance gives the true
centroid y. The theorem does not claim symmetry of lower-dimensional
integer boundary fibers or of the ambient convex body between integers.

## 6. Why q=0 is excluded

The non-atomic hypothesis at y is essential. For n=1,d=0 and
`C=[0,3]`, the source consists of the four integers 0,1,2,3. At y=1 its
closed-halfspace depth is one half, but its counting measure is not
symmetric about 1. The point mass on a through-y boundary prevents the
two opposite closed caps from both having mass exactly M/2. No q=0
extension is asserted.

## 7. Exact ambient thickening of a lower-dimensional symmetric extraction

Assume now that C is an ambient convex BODY. Fix y=(j,c) in S with
positive intrinsic reflection retention and put

    E=C intersect (2y-C), R=H_q(E intersect Lambda)>0.

If E is ambient-full, it is already a convex body with symmetric mixed
measure of mass R and true centroid y. If E is not ambient-full, its
base affine span `A=aff(pi(E))` is a proper affine subspace of R^n.
Here is a proof of this last assertion.

By symmetry, E has a positive q-dimensional own fiber at j: reflect
any positive fiber and take their Minkowski midpoint as in Section 5.
If pi(E) were full-dimensional, its symmetry about j would put j in
the interior of pi(E), and hence of pi(C). For an ambient convex body,
every base point in int(pi(C)) has a full d-dimensional fiber. Indeed
take an interior point of C, extend the segment in base space past the
specified interior base to another base in pi(C), and lift that segment;
the convex combination has the specified base and is an interior point
of C. Thus K_j has dimension d, giving q=d. The own d-dimensional fiber
of E and n independent base directions in pi(E) then force E to have
affine dimension n+d, a contradiction.

Since A is proper and pi(C) is bounded, the finitely many integer bases
of C outside A have a strictly positive minimum distance delta from A;
if there are none, choose any delta>0. Choose a small closed ambient ball
B contained in int(C), as close to y as necessary, such that:

  * every base point of B has distance less than delta from A;
  * all of pi(B) lies strictly on one side of a base hyperplane
    containing A.

Such a ball exists: int(C) approaches y, has open base projection, and
is not contained in the proper affine subspace A. First choose a nearby
interior point outside A, then choose a sufficiently small ball around it.
Define `D=conv(E union B)`. It is an actual convex body contained in C.

Every base of D has distance less than delta from A unless it already
lies in A, because E projects into A and distance to an affine subspace
is convex. Consequently all integer bases of D lie in A. The strict
one-sided base hyperplane makes the slice of D over A equal to E:
a convex combination using any positive B-weight has strictly positive
value of its defining affine functional, whereas bases in A have value
zero. Therefore

    D intersect Lambda=E intersect Lambda EXACTLY.  (10)

This full-dimensional D preserves the entire mixed source, not just an
approximation to its mass. Its intrinsic mixed mass is R, its true
centroid is y, and its local depth is one half.

## 8. Consequence for extraction, with the exact scope retained

For every 0<t<=M, when q>0 and C is an ambient body, the following are
equivalent:

  (a) Some actual mixed point has intrinsic reflection retention >=t.
  (b) Some convex body D subset C has H_q mixed mass >=t and true
      integer-base centroid whose local mixed depth is at least 1/2.

For (a) implies (b), use the symmetric intersection and, if necessary,
Section 7. For (b) implies (a), D has positive H_q mass, so its largest
integer fiber dimension is q. Apply the proved rigidity to D; its
positive source measure is symmetric and is contained in the original
reflection intersection at its centroid. Its mass is therefore at most
that original retention.

For d=1, gamma_d=1/2, so this is exactly the locally-Grünbaum-deep
extraction condition at any proposed retained threshold, for arbitrary
n. For d>1, gamma_d<1/2; this theorem concerns the strictly stronger
LOCAL HALF-depth condition and does not decide the proposed local
gamma_d extraction mechanism. No reflection lower bound or OC constant
is inferred from the equivalence.
